summary:
The Falkland Islands, a British Overseas Territory with its own Legislative Assembly, legislate locally. Same-sex activity has been legal since 1989 and the age of consent has been equal since 2005. Same-sex marriage and civil partnerships have been available since 29 April 2017; the bill passed the Legislative Assembly in March 2017 by 7 votes to 1, and the registrar general subsequently confirmed that it is law. Civil partnerships are open to opposite-sex couples as well as same-sex couples.

The Constitution Order 2008 bans discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation at Article 16. The provision covers sexual orientation only; the sources do not identify a gender-identity ground in the Constitution.

UK frameworks do not reach the Islands. The UK Equality Act 2010 and the Gender Recognition Act 2004 do not extend to the Falkland Islands, and the territory's own ordinances govern instead. These include the Crimes Ordinance 2014, which makes sexual-orientation hate-stirring an offence; the Crime and Public Order (Equality) Ordinance 2014, which provides sexual orientation as an aggravating factor in sentencing and recognises acquired gender under a UK Gender Recognition Certificate; and the Prisons Ordinance 2017.

The Crime and Public Order (Equality) Ordinance 2014 has permitted legal gender change since 2014. Gender recognition is not available on a self-identification basis, and no non-binary status is recognised.

The registrar general also confirmed that same-sex marriage is not legal in the South Georgia and South Sandwich Islands, a separate dependency for which the UK is responsible; the equality reform applies to the Falkland Islands themselves.
tangentialFactors:
The 2017 reform followed a public consultation in a territory of roughly 3,000 residents, which recorded 90 per cent support for same-sex marriage and 94 per cent for civil partnerships. The sources characterise local attitudes as largely positive, and the first Pride in Stanley took place in April 2017 alongside the marriage reform.

The legal position differs from Great Britain, where the Equality Act 2010, the Gender Recognition Act 2004 and UK case law on single-sex services operate. Those instruments have no application in the Falkland Islands, so a visitor who relies on Great Britain-based rights or precedent is relying on a framework that does not run here.

The United Kingdom remains responsible for defence of the territory, while the Legislative Assembly handles domestic legislation, including criminal and equality law.
localsOnly:
Stepchild adoption and joint adoption by same-sex couples have been available since 2017, the same year as the marriage reform.

Residents seeking legal gender change have been able to do so since 2014 under the Crime and Public Order (Equality) Ordinance 2014, which recognises acquired gender evidenced by a UK Gender Recognition Certificate. There is no self-identification route to recognition, and no non-binary marker or status is available.

Discrimination protection for residents rests on Article 16 of the Constitution Order 2008, which addresses sexual orientation, and on the sexual-orientation aggravating factor in the Crime and Public Order (Equality) Ordinance 2014. The Prisons Ordinance 2017 governs the territory's custodial arrangements.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources state that the Crimes Ordinance 2014 criminalises sexual-orientation hate-stirring but do not give the penalty ranges, the elements of the offence, or any reported prosecution. Enforcement of the constitutional non-discrimination guarantee and the sentencing aggravating factor is likewise unsourced here; whether either has been invoked in a decided case is unresolved.

No source in this inventory addresses facilities or bathroom access, healthcare provision for trans residents or visitors, immigration or security screening, name and gender markers on travel documents presented at entry, or documented incidents of violence against trans people. Those points should be treated as not sourced rather than as absent risk.

The exact commencement procedure for the 2017 marriage legislation is not detailed: the bill passed in March 2017 and marriage has been available from 29 April 2017, with the registrar general's reply confirming the law in June 2017. Whether gender recognition under the 2014 ordinance is available to persons who are not settled residents is not covered by the sources.
